# Chapter 1 Practice: Introduction to Chemistry

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/introduction.md`), grouped by objective and ordered easier → harder within each. 27 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 1.1a}} · *short answer* Identify which are pure substances and which are mixtures: (a) diamond; (b) milk; \(c) air; (d) wine.
:::
::: tab Answer
(a) Diamond is a **pure substance** (element: carbon). (b), \(c), and (d) — milk, air, and wine — are all **mixtures**: each combines multiple substances whose proportions can vary.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 1.1a}} · *multiple-choice* Which of the following is a compound rather than an element?

A. Oxygen gas ($\ce{O2}$)
B. Solid copper
C. Table salt ($\ce{NaCl}$)
D. Aluminum foil
:::
::: tab Answer
**C.** Table salt is sodium and chlorine chemically combined in a fixed 1:1 ratio — a compound. The other three each contain only one type of atom, making them elements.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 1.1a}} · *short answer* Stainless steel is uniform to the eye and can be made with different amounts of chromium. Classify it, and explain which single fact rules out "compound."
:::
::: tab Answer
**Homogeneous mixture.** Uniform appearance puts it in the *homogeneous* column, but the deciding fact is that the chromium content **can be varied** — a compound has a fixed ratio of its elements. Being able to change the proportions and still have the same material is the definition of a mixture.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 1.1b}} · *multiple-choice* Which of the following is an example of a physical property (not a change)?

A. Gasoline burns
B. Lead melts at 327 °C
C. A freshly cut apple turns brown
D. Dynamite explodes
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** A melting point is a physical property — melting itself is a physical change (no new substance forms). The other options describe chemical changes (combustion, browning/oxidation, explosion).
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 1.1b}} · *multiple-choice* Which of the following represents a chemical change?

A. Ice floats on liquid water
B. Breaking glass
C. A silver platter tarnishes
D. Mixing iron filings and sand at room temperature
:::
::: tab Answer
**C.** Tarnishing forms a new substance (silver sulfide) on the surface. The other options are physical changes or observations — no new substance is formed.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 1.1b}} · *short answer* Both of these produce a gas. Which is a chemical change, and what evidence separates them? (a) Dry ice sublimes into fog. (b) An antacid tablet fizzes in water.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(b) is the chemical change.** The fizzing produces carbon dioxide that did not exist before — a *new* substance formed from the reaction of the tablet's ingredients with water. In (a), the fog is the same $\ce{CO2}$ that was in the solid, just in a different state.

The lesson: "a gas appeared" is not evidence of a chemical change by itself. The question is whether the gas is a **new substance** or the same substance in a new state.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2a}} · *short answer* A block of aluminum has a mass of 2.7 kg on Earth. What would its mass be on the Moon? What would happen to its weight?
:::
::: tab Answer
Mass stays **2.7 kg** — mass measures the amount of matter, which doesn't change with location. Weight (the force of gravity on that mass) would **decrease to about one-sixth** of its Earth value, since the Moon's gravity is weaker.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2a}} · *workout* Convert 0.045 km to centimeters.
:::
::: tab Answer
Route it through the base unit (meters):
$$0.045\,\text{km}\times\frac{10^{3}\,\text{m}}{1\,\text{km}}\times\frac{1\,\text{cm}}{10^{-2}\,\text{m}}=4.5\times10^{3}\ \text{cm}$$
Check the direction: centimeters are far smaller than kilometers, so the number must get much larger — it did.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2a}} · *short answer* Which is larger, a nanometer or a picometer — and roughly how many picometers wide is a typical atom (about 100 pm)?
:::
::: tab Answer
A **nanometer** is larger: $1\,\text{nm}=10^{-9}$ m while $1\,\text{pm}=10^{-12}$ m, so 1 nm = 1000 pm. A typical atom at about 100 pm is therefore about **0.1 nm** across — which is why atomic sizes are usually quoted in picometers rather than nanometers.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2b}} · *workout* The density of iron is 7.87 g/cm³. What is the volume of 25.7 g of iron?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$V=\frac{m}{d}=\frac{25.7\,\text{g}}{7.87\,\text{g/cm}^3}=3.27\ \text{cm}^3$$
(3 significant figures, matching 25.7 g and 7.87 g/cm³.)
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2b}} · *workout* Mercury has a density of 13.6 g/mL. What is the mass of 5.00 mL of mercury?
:::
::: tab Answer
Rearranging $d=m/V$ gives $m=d\times V$:
$$m=13.6\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}\times5.00\,\text{mL}=68.0\ \text{g}$$
The mL cancel and leave grams, confirming the rearrangement was the right way up.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2b}} · *workout* A sample occupies 250 cm³. Express this volume in (a) mL and (b) L.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a)** $1\,\text{cm}^3=1\,\text{mL}$ exactly, so the volume is **250 mL** — no arithmetic needed.
**(b)** $250\,\text{mL}\times\dfrac{1\,\text{L}}{1000\,\text{mL}}=$ **0.250 L**.

The cm³ = mL identity is worth memorising: it lets you move between a volume calculated from dimensions and one read off a graduated cylinder with no conversion at all.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2c}} · *workout* Convert 25.00 °C to Kelvin.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$?\,\text{K}=(25.00+273.15)\,^\circ\text{C}\times\frac{1\,\text{K}}{1\,^\circ\text{C}}=298.15\ \text{K}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2c}} · *workout* Many home freezers maintain a temperature of 0.00 °F. Express this temperature in °C.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$?\,^\circ\text{C}=(0.00\,^\circ\text{F}-32\,^\circ\text{F})\times\frac{5\,^\circ\text{C}}{9\,^\circ\text{F}}=-17.8\ ^\circ\text{C}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 1.2c}} · *workout* Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C. Express this in kelvin, and explain why the kelvin value cannot be negative.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$?\,\text{K}=-196+273.15=77\ \text{K}$$
The kelvin scale starts at **absolute zero**, the lowest temperature physically possible, so no real temperature can fall below 0 K. Celsius zero is just the freezing point of water — an arbitrary reference with plenty of colder things below it. This is exactly why gas-law calculations (Chapter 5 onward) require kelvin: they use *ratios* of temperature, which only make sense on a scale with a true zero.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3a}} · *short answer* Express the number 0.0215 in scientific notation.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$0.0215=2.15\times10^{-2}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3a}} · *short answer* Rank the following values from smallest to largest: (a) 28600; (b) $1.21\times10^5$; \(c) $4.32\times10^{-6}$; (d) $7.20\times10^{-2}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Converting all to the same form: (a) $2.86\times10^4$, (b) $1.21\times10^5$, \(c) $4.32\times10^{-6}$, (d) $7.20\times10^{-2}$.

**\(c) < (d) < (a) < (b)**
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3a}} · *workout* Evaluate, giving each answer in proper scientific notation: (a) $(6.0\times10^{5})\div(2.0\times10^{2})$; (b) $1.20\times10^{4}+3.4\times10^{3}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a)** Division → divide the $N$ values, subtract the exponents:
$$\frac{6.0}{2.0}\times10^{5-2}=3.0\times10^{3}$$

**(b)** Addition → match the exponents *first*, then add:
$$1.20\times10^{4}+0.34\times10^{4}=1.54\times10^{4}$$

Note the two rules are different: (a) combines exponents, (b) requires them to match before you can do anything. Applying (a)'s rule to (b) is the classic error.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3b}} · *short answer* How many significant figures are in each: (a) 358 m; (b) 35.1 g; \(c) 0.932 kg; (d) 0.0068 m; (e) $9.320\times10^{23}$ molecules; (f) 3400 mL?
:::
::: tab Answer
(a) 3; (b) 3; \(c) 3; (d) 2; (e) 4; (f) 2 or 4 (ambiguous without a decimal point or scientific notation).
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3b}} · *short answer* How many significant figures are in each: (a) 0.00120 g; (b) 1.0080 s; \(c) 200. cm; (d) $2.0\times10^{3}$ kg?
:::
::: tab Answer
(a) **3** — leading zeros never count, but the trailing zero after a decimal does.
(b) **5** — zeros between nonzero digits always count, and so does the trailing zero after the decimal.
\(c) **3** — the written decimal point is the signal that the trailing zeros were measured.
(d) **2** — scientific notation removes all ambiguity; only the digits in $N$ count.

Compare \(c) with (f) in the previous question: "200." and "200" are different claims about precision, and the decimal point is the entire difference.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3c}} · *workout* Give each result with the correct number of significant figures: (a) $3245+1.649$; (b) $54.3-3.32$; \(c) $3.14\times2.5$; (d) $0.0029\div92.1$.
:::
::: tab Answer
(a) $3247$ (decimal-place rule: 3245 has 0 decimal places). (b) $51.0$ (1 decimal place, matching 54.3). \(c) $7.8$ (2 sig figs, matching 2.5). (d) $0.000031$, i.e. $3.1\times10^{-5}$ (2 sig figs, matching 0.0029).
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3c}} · *short answer* A student weighs the same object four times and gets 10.51, 10.53, 10.52, and 10.52 g. The object's true mass, from a certified reference, is 10.80 g. Are these measurements precise? Accurate?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Precise** — the four values cluster tightly together (within 0.02 g of each other). **Not accurate** — all four values are about 0.27–0.29 g below the true mass of 10.80 g, likely indicating a systematic error (e.g., an uncalibrated balance).

This is the most dangerous combination in a lab: nothing in the data itself reveals the problem, because the readings agree beautifully with each other. Only comparison against a known standard exposes it.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 1.4a}} · *workout* The mass of a competition frisbee is 125 g. Convert its mass to ounces, given 1 oz = 28.349 g.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$125\,\text{g}\times\frac{1\,\text{oz}}{28.349\,\text{g}}=4.41\ \text{oz}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 1.4a}} · *workout* A recipe calls for 1.5 cups of water. Given 1 cup = 236.6 mL and water's density is 1.00 g/mL, what mass of water is this in kilograms?
:::
::: tab Answer
Chain three factors — cups → mL → g → kg:
$$1.5\,\text{cup}\times\frac{236.6\,\text{mL}}{1\,\text{cup}}\times\frac{1.00\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{mL}}\times\frac{1\,\text{kg}}{1000\,\text{g}}=0.35\ \text{kg}$$
Track the cancellation: cup against cup, mL against mL, g against g — leaving kg. Two significant figures, because 1.5 has two and limits the result.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 25
{{sp[info] Objective 1.4a}} · *workout* What is the density, in g/mL, of an antifreeze sample if 4.00 qt of it weighs 9.26 lb? (1 lb = 453.59 g; 1 L = 1.0567 qt)
:::
::: tab Answer
Convert mass and volume separately, then divide:
$$9.26\,\text{lb}\times\frac{453.59\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{lb}}=4200\,\text{g} \qquad 4.00\,\text{qt}\times\frac{1\,\text{L}}{1.0567\,\text{qt}}\times\frac{1000\,\text{mL}}{1\,\text{L}}=3786\,\text{mL}$$
$$\frac{4200\,\text{g}}{3786\,\text{mL}}=1.11\ \text{g/mL}$$
A plausibility check: antifreeze should be slightly denser than water (1.00 g/mL), and 1.11 g/mL is exactly that.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 26
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3b}} · *workout* A thermometer is marked every 1 °C. The mercury sits about halfway between the 24 and 25 marks. Record the temperature, state how many significant figures it has, and identify which digits are certain and which is estimated.
:::
::: tab Answer
Record **24.5 °C**, which has **3 significant figures**.

The 2 and the 4 are **certain** — the markings give them to you directly. The 5 is **estimated**, judged by eye between two marks.

Recording 24 °C would discard information you could genuinely see. Recording 24.50 °C would claim a hundredths digit that no instrument marked in whole degrees can support. The rule is the same for every analog scale: every certain digit, plus exactly one estimated digit.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 27
{{sp[info] Objective 1.3c}} · *short answer* Two thermometers are used to measure a bath whose true temperature is 25.0 °C. Thermometer P reads 27.4, 27.5, 27.4, 27.5 °C. Thermometer Q reads 24.1, 26.2, 25.4, 24.3 °C. Which is more precise, which is more accurate, and which would you rather rely on for a single unrepeated measurement?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Thermometer P is far more precise** — its four readings span only 0.1 °C. It is **not accurate**: every reading is about 2.5 °C too high, so it is almost certainly miscalibrated.

**Thermometer Q is more accurate** — its readings average 25.0 °C, the true value — but it is **imprecise**, scattering over 2.1 °C.

For a single unrepeated measurement, **Q is the safer choice**, and this is the counter-intuitive part. P will be wrong by about 2.5 °C every single time, with no way to detect it from the data. Q will be wrong by a smaller amount on average, and its visible scatter warns you not to over-trust any one reading.

P's fault is correctable by calibration against a known standard; Q's is not, but Q's is at least visible. A precise instrument that is never checked against a standard is the most dangerous instrument in the lab.
:::
::::
